title: Foley v. Interactive Data Corp.
lead: An employee reports troubling information about a new supervisor and is later discharged despite alleged assurances of job security. His complaint presents three different routes to recovery, which the California Supreme Court treats separately.

actors.name: Daniel D. Foley
actors.role: Former employee alleging wrongful discharge and contractual job security.

actors.name: Richard Earnest
actors.role: Former supervisor to whom Foley disclosed information.

actors.name: Robert Kuhne
actors.role: New supervisor whose background Foley discussed and who delivered the resignation-or-discharge choice.

proceedings: The trial court sustained demurrers to all three claims without leave to amend, and the Court of Appeal affirmed.
The California Supreme Court affirmed dismissal of public-policy and tortious-covenant claims, reversed dismissal of the implied-contract claim, and remanded.
limits: This transforms the canonical historical brief without a fresh opinion audit or certification of current employment law. Allegations were assumed on demurrer, not proved. The Court reserved damages for the surviving claim and prospective versus retroactive application. No modern rule on express at-will writings is inferred.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Years of work allegedly produce an understanding of job security
sections.cue: What communications supported more than at-will employment?
paragraphs: Interactive Data Corporation hired Daniel Foley in June 1976 as an assistant product manager at $18,500. It required a writing restricting competition and requiring disclosure and assignment of computer-related information and innovations for one year after termination. That writing did not state permissible discharge grounds.

Foley alleged that over six years and nine months he received promotions, raises, bonuses, favorable reviews, and assurances that adequate performance meant continued employment. He became Los Angeles branch manager at $56,164 annually. Written guidelines allegedly specified dismissal grounds and a mandatory seven-step termination procedure. He understood those protections to apply and declined other jobs in reliance on security.

sections.title: Foley reports a supervisor’s investigation and later faces discharge
sections.cue: Which facts were allegations rather than adjudicated motives?
paragraphs: In January 1983, Foley privately told former supervisor Richard Earnest that new supervisor Robert Kuhne was under Federal Bureau of Investigation scrutiny for embezzlement from Bank of America. Foley alleged he acted for Interactive Data’s benefit because it conducted confidential financial-community business. Earnest told him to disregard the rumors.

In March, Kuhne announced replacement for performance reasons and a possible Massachusetts transfer. Foley was told refusing might mean demotion rather than firing. Later discussions offered continued branch management under a performance plan, but at the meeting intended to present it, Kuhne instead demanded resignation or discharge. Foley received a $6,762 merit bonus two days before termination.

These allegations were assumed true on demurrer. Employer assertions that Foley sought to oust Kuhne and rejected an available transfer were not reviewable facts. Kuhne’s September 1983 guilty plea was a later event, distinct from what Foley knew when he spoke.

sections.title: Three dismissed causes of action reach the Supreme Court
sections.cue: Why does the public-policy claim fail?
paragraphs: Foley sought compensatory and punitive damages through discharge contrary to public policy, breach of an implied agreement requiring good cause, and tortious breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing. The trial court sustained demurrers without leave to amend, and the Court of Appeal affirmed all three.

Chief Justice Lucas explained that Labor Code § 2922’s at-will presumption did not authorize violations of fundamental public policy. Tameny recognized an independent legal duty, exemplified by refusing an employer’s demand to commit a crime, without requiring a job-security contract.

Foley invoked an employee-agent’s duty to relay material business information. The court did not finally decide whether that duty arose from statutory ordinary care or uncodified agency law, or whether every public-policy claim required a statutory or constitutional source. Even assuming such a source, the pleaded duty needed to serve fundamental public interests.

The majority viewed this disclosure as serving Interactive Data’s private interests, unlike refusing crimes, reporting to authorities, or disclosing unsafe conditions. Parties could agree to dispense with adverse-background reporting about colleagues but could not contract around prohibitions such as perjury or antitrust violations. It upheld dismissal on these allegations without rejecting all internal whistleblowing claims.

sections.title: The alleged course of conduct can support an implied good-cause bargain
sections.cue: Why were separate consideration and reciprocal restraints unnecessary?
paragraphs: The job-security allegation was more accurately implied in fact than an express oral promise: Foley relied on conduct and representations rather than particular words establishing good cause. Ordinary contract law allowed inference of actual understanding. Section 2922 supplied a presumption, not a prohibition on implied discharge limits.

Services could support multiple promises, including wages and protection against arbitrary dismissal; separate consideration was not invariably necessary. Nor did consideration require equivalent restrictions on Foley’s right to leave. Historical treatment of permanent employment did not prevent enforceable good-cause agreements.

Policies, practices, longevity, assurances, and industry customs could show such an understanding. Six years and nine months permitted relevant conduct, without establishing a minimum tenure. Oblique language alone would not suffice, but the combined assurances, promotions, favorable treatment, and written procedure could support Foley’s claim. Postemployment competition and information commitments supplied additional evidence of a continuing relationship, though indispensable extra consideration was not required.

The court found sufficient allegations to permit proof, not a proved contract or established absence of good cause. Unlike writings expressly declaring at-will status, the alleged writings were silent about discharge grounds; broader conflicts between express at-will language and implied modification remained unresolved.

sections.title: The one-year statute of frauds does not eliminate that contract claim
sections.cue: What counts as possible performance within a year?
paragraphs: Civil Code § 1624 applied only where the terms made performance within one year impossible. An indefinite good-cause employment arrangement could be completed within that period if Foley left or the employer discharged for cause. Expected longevity was different from impossibility, and the inquiry looked forward from formation rather than backward from actual service.

The Court of Appeal’s reliance on Newfield confused anticipated duration and differing termination rights with that test. Relying on White Lighting, longstanding interpretations, and legislative adoption of narrowly construed language, the court disapproved inconsistent Newfield reasoning. Foley could proceed despite the alleged agreement’s oral or implied character.

sections.title: The covenant protects contractual benefits without supplying this tort remedy
sections.cue: Why does the majority reject the insurance analogy?
paragraphs: The implied covenant applied to employment contracts, but the majority declined to carry over insurance law’s exception allowing tort damages. Contract law protected agreed expectations; tort law enforced wider social duties. Insurance involved protection against calamity, bargaining inequality, and distinctive insurer obligations. A person could not buy replacement coverage for an incurred loss, while a discharged employee could seek replacement work and had a mitigation duty. Employers did not sell loss protection or perform the same quasi-public function and ordinarily benefited from retaining capable workers.

Predictability, business stability, extensive motive disputes, and existing statutory and public-policy protections supported caution. Contract damages might be inadequate, but possible expanded contract recovery, fees, arbitration, or legislation were alternatives the court did not adopt here. It left the surviving claim’s damages measure undecided.

Seaman’s narrow tort involving bad-faith denial of a contract’s existence did not extend to disputes about good cause under an acknowledged agreement. Nor could the covenant convert every genuine at-will relationship into a good-cause one; it protected benefits actually promised. Cleary and related decisions were disapproved insofar as they authorized tort remedies for employment-covenant breach.

sections.title: Three dissenting writers challenge the limits on employee protection
sections.cue: What did the divided judgment preserve?
paragraphs: Justice Broussard agreed with the first two results but saw tort protection as established appellate law. Employee dependence, dignity, security, and distress made the insurance analogy persuasive; knowing arbitrary violations differed from innocent breach. He criticized removing remedies while invoking legislative restraint and suggested exploring foreseeable emotional-distress damages in contract, without deciding their availability here.

Justice Kaufman likewise accepted Parts I and II but favored tort remedies for willful, malicious discharge. Good faith was a legally imposed duty; vulnerability could equal that of insureds. He defended common-law development and considered Koehrer’s good-faith/probable-cause distinction workable without making every mistaken breach tortious.

Justice Mosk agreed with those views except their approval of the public-policy dismissal. Reporting possible supervisory criminal wrongdoing, he thought, benefited society as well as the company. Protecting reports to police while permitting retaliation for first approaching an employer was incongruous.

On December 29, 1988, the court affirmed the public-policy and tortious-covenant dismissals, reversed the implied-contract dismissal, and remanded. Lucas, Panelli, Arguelles, and Eagleson supported the majority throughout; public policy divided six to one, contract revival was unanimous, and rejection of covenant tort damages divided four to three. No contract or damages were finally established. Prospective versus retroactive application remained reserved because it was neither briefed nor argued.
